title: The status observer's control messages are fake log envelopes with string kinds and a JSON round trip
reason: The string control kinds (status.rs:29-42), `control()` (921-932), the `Unknown(name) if name ==` guards (1032-1050), the JSON payload for SUBJECT (841-853) and the separate `closing: mpsc::Sender<Published>` channel are all as described. The proposal is harder than stated. The queue is `log::Injector` (log/src/read.rs:560-584). It holds `Envelope`s inside the log watcher's queue, which re-reads the log on catch-up but keeps pushed lines, and doors also uses it (doors/src/client/level.rs, session.rs). A typed item therefore means changing the log crate across a crate boundary. Also, `Fold::subject` compares the call against `latest`, the raw JSON payload of the log line ('exactly the call payload the log wrote'), so a typed Subject still needs serialising or parsing for that comparison. The problem is real (a closed set held in strings), but the fix is wider than this crate and saves less than 35 lines.
evidence: Four internal commands (LIVE, STOP, SUBJECT and CLOSING, defined at status.rs:29-42) are sent as `Envelope`s with `EventKind::from_name("status_*")` and an empty session id (the `control()` helper at 921-932), then recognised by string comparison in `EventKind::Unknown(name) if name == STOP` guards (1032-1050). SUBJECT serialises a typed `ToolCallRequested` to a JSON Value and puts it in `payload["call"]` (841-853). `Fold::subject` then reads `payload.get("call")` and `payload.get("subject")` back out and compares raw JSON objects (284-298). Close requests travel on a second channel (`closing: mpsc::Sender<Published>`) next to the injected CLOSING line. This is a closed set expressed as strings, and typed data that loses its type in the process.
prop: Give the observer one typed queue, for example `enum Input { Line(Envelope), Live, Stop, Subject { call: ToolCallRequested, subject: Option<String> }, Closing(Published) }`. Ordering with log lines can be kept by having the watcher's injector carry this enum, or by having log::Injector take a generic item. That removes control(), the string guards, the JSON round trip and the second channel.

title: Git `.git` pointer and common-directory discovery is written four times, under three different rules
reason: The two ancestor walks really are the same: git.rs:26-56 and gh_owner.rs:211-243 each check for a symlink, then a dir, then a file, treat NotFound as continue, call is_bare, then pop. The pointer parsing really does differ: git.rs uses a 512-byte cap and File::open; gh_owner uses 512 bytes, rustix NOFOLLOW, requires a regular file and exactly one line; sandbox read_capped uses 4096 bytes and takes the first line trimmed. baseline.rs:287-289 does reach into super::super::read_capped and pointer_gitdir. But the sandbox code is not the same algorithm. It has no ancestor walk and looks only at workspace/.git. rooted_path falls back to a lexical path when the target is missing, because deny rules must still name a path that does not exist. It does not require the target to sit under a .git component; instead it checks the back-pointer with belongs_to_workspace and is_git_layout. And it returns grant directories, not a yes/no. On Linux it reads the text from baseline entries, but belongs_to_workspace still reads from disk. So one shared reader and one shared walk are sound, but a single GitLayout resolver shared with the classifier guards would have to keep two different policies: strict fail-closed for classification, lenient lexical for sandbox grants. 120 lines is too high. Realistically the walk merge saves about 30 lines and unifying the pointer reader about 30.
evidence: The ancestor walk is written twice. git::repository_ok (git.rs:26-56) and gh_owner::common_dir (gh_owner.rs:211-243) walk upward over `.git` the same way: a symlinked `.git` refuses, a directory is accepted, a file goes to the pointer parser, NotFound continues, an is_bare check runs, then pop. The pointer parser is written three times with different rules. git::gitfile_ok (git.rs:84-122, 39 lines) caps the read at 512 bytes and opens with File::open, which follows symlinks. gh_owner's gitdir_common, commondir_common, parse_pointer, read_pointer and read_bounded (gh_owner.rs:251-343, about 90 lines) cap at 512 bytes, open with O_NOFOLLOW and accept exactly one line. sandbox/mod.rs has read_capped, pointer_gitdir, common_dir and belongs_to_workspace (lines 903-938); it caps at 4096 bytes and takes the first line trimmed, so it accepts input the other two refuse. Inside sandbox/mod.rs itself, discover_git (macOS, 866-900) and recorded_git_roots (Linux, 603-634) repeat the same sequence: pointer, then gitdir, then commondir, then belongs_to_workspace, then is_git_layout. They differ only in where the text comes from (disk or baseline entries). baseline.rs:287-289 reaches into the parent module for `super::super::read_capped` and `pointer_gitdir`.
prop: Make shell/git.rs the one module that reads git layout. It would expose a single bounded, NOFOLLOW pointer reader; a `GitLayout { gitdir, commondir }` resolver that takes a text source (a closure, so the baseline-backed Linux path and the on-disk macOS path share it); and the ancestor walk. repository_ok, gh_owner's common_dir, the sandbox and the baseline would call it. This also settles which of the three parsing rules is correct, a question that currently differs by caller.

title: File tools reach into a getter/setter `Shared` and each repeats the resolve, lock, recheck and land sequence
reason: The accessors at files.rs:465-508 are as described. write.rs:87-109 and edit.rs:108-128 do repeat resolve, lock, re-resolve, judged and recheck. write.rs:123-139 and edit.rs:161-177 repeat land, set_seen, note_approved_write and two CouldNotWrite mappings, and the three effects() bodies match. One difference matters, though: write captures `self.shared.seen(&key)` between the first resolve and taking the lock (write.rs:95), so that two replaces both based on the same read cannot both land. Edit does not do this, and read takes no lock. A single open_checked therefore has to return the pre-lock seen hash, or offer a hook before the lock. As stated, the proposal would lose that ordering. The accessors also cannot all become private: read uses images(), and write uses seen() for its stale check. With those caveats the commit() and judge() helpers would work, but the saving is smaller than 70 lines.
evidence: Shared (files.rs:465-508) exposes workspace(), locks(), images(), note_judged(), judged(), seen(), set_seen() and note_approved_write() as pub(crate) accessors, and each caller must call them in the right order. Before the work, write.rs:87-109 (23 lines) and edit.rs:108-128 (21 lines) both resolve the path, take `locks.lock(&key)`, resolve again, read `judged(&raw)` and call `tool_util::recheck(.., Some(&key), .., Act::Write)`; read.rs:120-134 does the same without the lock. After the work, write.rs:123-139 and edit.rs:161-177 are the same 17 lines: land, set_seen(hash_bytes), note_approved_write, and two CouldNotWrite mappings. All three `effects` functions (read.rs:93-98, write.rs:70-75, edit.rs:87-93) are resolve, then note_judged, then declare.
prop: Give Shared two deep operations and make the accessors private. The first is `open_checked(&self, raw, Act) -> Result<Checked, FileError>`, which resolves, optionally locks, re-resolves and rechecks, and returns the path plus the guard. The second is `commit(&self, path, bytes) -> Result<(), FileError>`, which lands the bytes, records the hash and advances the baseline. Also add `judge(&self, raw, Effect, reversible)` for effects(). Then the order of operations that the stale-file and protected-path rules depend on lives in one place, and read, write and edit keep only their own logic.

title: `Finished` holds stop reasons as independent flags that can contradict each other
reason: Finished (command.rs:40-60) does keep stop, indeterminate, held_open, capped and flooded as separate fields. pre_end_of (shell.rs:1418-1444) fixes their precedence with an if-chain, and docs/code-quality.md:246 forbids structs whose fields can contradict each other. So the rule violation is real. The proposed enum does not cover the states the code actually produces. drive.rs:406 sets indeterminate when host_lost is true even with no stop, so 'indeterminate' is not only a property of a stop; the proposal's Exited/Stopped split has no place for a lost host with no stop. keeper_finished (hosted.rs:274-291) can set stop=Timeout and capped=true at the same time. And background.rs:861-866 deliberately reads stop==Timeout before the capped override is applied, to build the TimedOutMoved hint. An enum would need to keep that secondary fact, or the background code would need restructuring. The direction is right, but the variant set has to be redesigned. The net line count is small.
evidence: Finished (command.rs:40-60) has `stop: Option<StopKind>` (Timeout or Cancel), but cap and flood, which are also stops, sit beside it as `capped: bool` and `flooded: bool`. `indeterminate` is documented as 'a stop ended with the pipe still open' and `held_open` as 'a normal end', yet both are free bools. drive.rs:406-407 has to derive them as `indeterminate: host_lost || (stopped && ..)` and `held_open: !stopped && ..`. keeper_finished (hosted.rs:274-291) sets `capped` while leaving `stop` None. pre_end_of (shell.rs:1418-1444) resolves the ambiguity with an if-chain that fixes the precedence: capped, then flooded, then indeterminate, then stop. background.rs:854 re-checks `!capped && !flooded && stop == Some(Cancel) && !indeterminate`. docs/code-quality.md, under 'Types', calls this 'a struct whose fields can contradict each other'.
prop: Replace the four flags with an enum, for example `End::Exited { held_open } | End::Stopped { why: Timeout | Cancel | Cap | Flood, indeterminate } | End::Unreaped`. pre_end_of becomes a direct match, and the precedence rules are carried by the type instead of by an if-chain.

title: The grep match side-file format is declared twice, in two modules
reason: search/matches.rs:20-27 declares Record<'a> with Cow fields and Serialize, and also holds MATCHES_ENV and LIMIT. shell/matches.rs:42-51 declares a second Record with the same five fields, using Deserialize and deny_unknown_fields; it also holds MatchDir and read(). shell.rs:943 passes crate::search::matches::LIMIT, and the env constant is used from command.rs, hosted.rs and spawn.rs. Both halves are in the same crate. matches_tests.rs tests only the writer's bytes; I found no round-trip test between writer and reader. A single Record<'a> with Cow fields can derive both Serialize and Deserialize, so the merge works. The saving is small.
evidence: search/matches.rs declares the writer's `Record { path, line, text, spans, context }` (Serialize), together with MATCHES_ENV and LIMIT. shell/matches.rs:42-51 declares a second `Record` with the same five fields (Deserialize, deny_unknown_fields), plus MatchDir and the reader. shell.rs:941 joins the two halves by reaching into `crate::search::matches::LIMIT`. Adding a field means editing both structs in step, and nothing checks that they agree.
prop: Move MatchDir, the writer, the reader and one shared Record into a single matches module (under search/ or at crate level). The shell then calls `matches::read(&dir)` without knowing the limit or the file name.

title: assemble_session repeats about 300 lines between its resume arm and its new-session arm
reason: I opened session_command.rs. assemble_session starts at 698. The Resume arm runs 713-1218 and the fresh arm starts at 1219. Both arms call quota_readers (801/1341), Delegates::new (802/1342), SkillSet::new (816/1359), web_search (818/1361), finish_processes, session_tools (834/1395), SessionOffer::new (865/1432), diag.attach (881/1455), keeper.observe (883/1463), command_update_wiring (989/1542) and reload::State::new (994/1547). Only the resume arm has resume_with_timing and the handover (905). Only the fresh arm has Log::create (1441) and open_with_timing (1464). I count 8 combine_close_result calls and 11 servers.stop() calls. I re-ran difflib on the stripped arms and got 305 matching lines, not 306. Many of those are bare braces and `);`, so the real saving is nearer 150-200 than 250. There are also small differences the merged module must carry: the resume arm uses folded.workspace for SkillSet and session_tools, and the clock source differs (the fresh arm can take the case-run clock). Neither blocks the proposal.
evidence: `assemble_session` runs from line 698 to 1823, so it is one 1,125-line function. The Start::Resume arm is lines 713-1218 (507 lines). The New/Delegate/Rewound arm is lines 1219-1811 (592 lines). After stripping indentation, difflib finds 306 identical lines between the two arms, in the same order. The repeated steps are: the 34-field `Parts` destructure (727 and 1297); `quota_readers` (801 and 1341); `Delegates::new` (802 and 1342); `SkillSet::new` (816 and 1359); `builtin::web_search` (818 and 1361); the `pending_mcp` None check plus `finish_processes` (825 and 1386); `mcp_servers::session_tools` with 19 arguments (834 and 1395); `SessionOffer::new` (865 and 1432); `diag.attach` (881 and 1455); `keeper.observe` (883 and 1463); the whole `session.*` and `extensions.*` wiring block; `command_update_wiring`; `reload::State::new` with 17 arguments (994 and 1547); and the shutdown/commit/close error ladder. `combine_close_result(.., close(session, log, &home, dir.path(), &workspace, &*clock, &keeper))` is written out 8 times, and `servers.stop()` 11 times. The arms really differ in only three ways: the resume arm opens an existing log (`Session::resume_with_timing`), the new arm creates one (`Log::create` + `Session::open_with_timing`), the resume arm runs the keeper handover, and each ends with a different `Loop::*` constructor.
prop: Make session assembly one deeper module, for example `session_command/assembly.rs`. Its single entry would take `Parts` plus a small `Opening` value: either 'resume this log and fold' or 'create a log for this fresh start'. That value would answer the three questions that really vary: how the log and the `Session` are opened, whether a keeper handover runs, and which `Loop` constructor builds the loop. The shared wiring would then run once. Put the 8 close-and-combine sites behind one guard or helper that owns `servers`, `session`, `log` and `keeper`. `Parts` would then be read in one place instead of being destructured twice.

title: run_new turns Option arguments into the Start enum, and assemble_session turns it straight back into Options
reason: The evidence holds. The (parent, rewound) match is at 662-684, the 8-tuple re-unpack and unreachable! are at 1222-1285, the third match on (rewound, parent) is at 1657, and the r#loop::Session literal appears at 1145, 1661, 1680, 1694 and 1706. One thing the proposal misses: rewind.rs:192, a fork, passes Some(parent) and Some(rewound) together. run_new also uses parent.is_some() for StartupAdmission::for_run before Start is built (line 557). So FreshKind::Rewound would lose the 'started as a delegate' bit unless the code reads it from Continuation::Fork { parent } or the kind keeps it. The redesign works once that is kept.
evidence: `run_new` takes `parent: Option<Parent>`, `rewound: Option<Rewound>`, `case_inputs` and `supervised` as separate positional arguments (14 arguments in all). At lines 662-684 it matches on `(parent, rewound)` to build `Start::Delegate`, `Start::Rewound` or `Start::New`. `assemble_session` then matches those three variants (lines 1222-1286) to rebuild an 8-tuple of the same Options, padding with `None`/`false`. It needs `unreachable!("a resumed start cannot assemble as new")` at line 1285, the kind of runtime check docs/code-quality.md says marks a type that is too loose. At line 1657 it matches `(rewound, parent)` a third time to pick a `Loop` constructor. The `r#loop::Session { log, provider, model, prompt, inbox, tools: capped(..), permissions }` literal is written out 5 times (1145, 1661, 1680, 1694, 1706). The three fresh variants all carry the same `id`, `workspace: WorkspaceStart` and `inherited` fields (lines 105-124).
prop: Change `Start` to `Fresh { id, workspace, inherited, kind: FreshKind }` plus `Resume(..)`, where `FreshKind` is `New { supervised, case_inputs } | Delegate(Parent) | Rewound(Rewound)`. Have callers pass a `FreshKind` instead of the Option pair. Then the tuple re-unpacking and the `unreachable!` go away. The final `Loop` choice becomes one `match kind`, with the `r#loop::Session` built once before it.

title: A worktree opener reaches run_new through a thread-local, and run_new_with exists only to set it
reason: The thread-local OPENED and OpenedHold (24-50), run_new_with (1823-1858), opened_hold_tests (1941-1983) and the debt comment are all as described. The five run_new callers each map Err through report. Deleting the thread-local in favour of an explicit argument is sound. Folding report into the entry point would not work as stated. In new_session (504-531), report has to run after isolation.end(), and the isolate and set_current_dir failures are reported before run_new is ever reached. So report cannot simply move inside run_new.
evidence: `thread_local! OPENED`, the `OpenedHold` drop guard (lines 24-50), `run_new_with` (lines 1823-1858, a 15-argument copy of `run_new`'s signature that only sets the thread-local and forwards), and the inline `opened_hold_tests` (1941-1983) all exist so that `run_new` keeps its signature. A comment at line 24 records this as debt. `run_new` reads the hidden slot at line 550, so a caller has to know to go through `run_new_with` to get the worktree's create line written. Of the 5 direct `run_new` callers (rewind.rs:192, 362, 469; continue_session.rs:82; session_command.rs:460), every one immediately maps `Err` through `session_command::report(signals, failure)`. Fold the `report` mapping into the entry point, and collect the 14 positional arguments into one `NewRun` struct with defaults, so the callers stop writing out runs of `None, None, false, Vec::new()`.

title: tui_extensions.rs repeats its extension-call failure handling four times and its winner-picking three times
reason: The four failure-handling copies in run_key, on_click, on_focus and run_tui_command are real. They differ in the Ok type (bool vs ()), the return value, and the de-duplication set (on_focus uses focus_hooks with a FocusNoticeKey), so a shared helper should take only the Err side. render and render_animated are near copies, but one calls vm.call and the other vm.call_animated, and their returns differ. The single select() proposal overstates the sameness. key_winner checks the configured winner first: a configured name that is not a contender yields None with no notice. fills_for lets a lone contender win before it looks at configured, and adds the configured name to its conflict message. command_winner has no configured winner and skips the compatibility gate when there is no session (documented in docs/extensions.md). A shared helper needs parameters for these orderings, so it saves less than claimed.
evidence: `run_key` (949-1000), `on_click` (1001-1049), `on_focus` (1050-1089) and `run_tui_command` (1104-1151) each hand-write the same 25-line match on the result of a call into the extension's Lua VM. On `TuiTimeout` they set `candidate.off` and push an `extension_failed` 'passed its X timeout' notice. On `TuiOff` they do nothing. On any other error they push a `hook_failed` notice, de-duplicated through a set. The four copies differ only in the verb (key binding, click handler, focus handler, command) and the key used for de-duplication. Winner-picking is written three times: `key_winner` (323-358) with `key_contenders` (292-317), `command_winner` (365-422), and the non-key branch of `fills_for` (753-800). Each one filters out switched-off candidates, reports incompatible ones through `notice_incompatible`, lets the configured winner or a lone contender win, and otherwise inserts a `ConflictNoticeKey` and pushes `command_conflict`. `render` (819-864) and `render_animated` (869-933) are also near copies: the same two `NotForSession` early returns, the same `built` closure and the same line mapping.
prop: Add one `Composite::called(candidate, extension, what, seen_key, result)` that maps a VM call's `Result` to the notice and to switching the extension off, and call it from the four handlers. Add one `select(contenders, configured, slot) -> Option<String>` that holds the filter, configured, lone and conflict logic for keys, commands and slots, with only the conflict wording passed in. Have `render` call `render_animated`'s body with no frame, or share a helper for the selection and the closure.

title: About 660 lines in tui_extensions.rs encode the tui crate's own types to JSON, away from where those types are defined
reason: Lines 1174-1834 are the encoders. I count 28 `*_value` functions, not 33; with helpers such as insert_present, call_status_str, with_changed_by and with_recipient it is about 32. None of them touches other main modules. tui depends on serde_json (Cargo.toml:18) and defines every encoded type in tui::ext::input. The encoding builds a serde_json::Value and needs no VM, so it can move without breaking the rule at the top of tui/src/ext.rs that tui depends on no VM crate. The proposal is feasible.
evidence: Lines 1174-1834 are 33 `*_value` functions (`input_value`, `session_value`, `ledger_value`, `entry_value`, `call_value` and others). Each turns one `tui::ext` borrowed type (`RendererInput`, `TurnEntry`, `SessionCard`, `LedgerRow`, ...) into the `serde_json::Value` the Lua renderer receives. Nothing else in main uses them, and they touch no other main module (`grep crate::` in the file finds nothing). The `tui` crate already depends on serde_json (crates/tui/Cargo.toml:18) and defines every type being encoded. So today, adding a field to a `tui::ext` card means editing a second crate. The file's other ~1,000 lines (slot selection, `Composite`) are a separate concern. docs/architecture.md:68 says main holds 'No feature logic'.
prop: Move the encoder into `tui::ext`, either as `RendererInput::to_value()` or as a `tui/src/ext/value.rs` module, so the shape the Lua renderer sees lives next to the types. tui_extensions.rs then keeps only the loader and the `Composite` adapter, at about 1,170 lines, and could be split further by moving `Composite` into its own file.

title: Notice codes and slot kinds in tui_extensions.rs are bare strings
reason: I count 29 pushes: extension_failed 19, command_conflict 5, hook_failed 4, extension_incompatible 1. (String, String) appears 6 times. docs/code-quality.md line 146 names a notice code as an example of a closed set that must be an enum when it crosses a crate boundary. The tui side converts straight back with ErrorCode::from_name(&code) (tui/src/app.rs:921 and others). contract::ErrorCode already has CommandConflict, ExtensionFailed, ExtensionIncompatible and HookFailed, so the traits can carry ErrorCode directly. The key:/command: string prefixes are as described.
evidence: The file pushes 29 notices as `("<code>".into(), message)`, using only four distinct codes: `extension_failed`, `extension_incompatible`, `command_conflict` and `hook_failed`. They travel to the tui crate as `Vec<(String, String)>` through `Load::load` and `Renderer::take_pending` (crates/tui/src/ext.rs:208, 260). That `(String, String)` type appears 6 times in this file. docs/code-quality.md, 'Types', names 'a notice code' as the example of a closed set that must be an enum when it crosses a crate boundary. Slot kinds are also packed into strings with prefixes: `format!("key:{canonical}")` and `slot.strip_prefix("key:")` at 744, and `format!("command:{name}")` at 1113. Comments at 1029-1031 and 1110-1112 argue that a colon can never collide.
prop: Have the tui crate's `Load` and `Renderer` traits carry the existing `contract` notice-code enum, or a new `tui::ext::NoticeCode`, instead of `String`. Model the slot as `enum SlotKey { Drawable(String), Key(String), Command(String) }`, so the de-duplication sets are keyed by type rather than by string prefix.

title: reload::State exposes 29 pub(crate) fields, takes 17 constructor arguments, and is implemented across two files
reason: The 29 pub(crate) fields (175-232), the 17-argument new (340) returning a 5-tuple, the reads of reload.sandbox and reload.sources.workspace at 1018-1019 and 1571-1572, and the impl in mcp_servers.rs:576 that touches the 8 named fields are all as described. What actually needs the crate visibility is mcp_servers.rs's impl block and session_command's reads. Session_command can also clone sandbox before passing it to new. title: Configuration layers are named by hand-written strings, and a parallel Layer enum needs mapping functions

title: session_tools takes 19 positional arguments, and its Option protection is None only in tests
reason: session_tools (352) takes 19 arguments and returns a 4-tuple. Both product calls pass Some(protection); mcp_servers_tests.rs passes None. title: relay/ack.rs hand-writes about 570 lines of serde visitors to read four fields of an acknowledgement
reason: The visitors are verbose as described, and LenientString and LenientU64 are near copies. A derived Deserialize fails with 'duplicate field', which loses the whole Ack. A generic Lenient<T> that 'tries T, otherwise drains' cannot rewind a streaming serde_json deserializer without buffering into a Value. ack.rs:121-125 deliberately avoids building a Value tree. Swapping Validate for IgnoredAny also changes behaviour. IgnoredAny's visit_seq and visit_map recurse through deserialize_ignored_any, which skips nested values rather than parsing them. The Validate doc (ack.rs:612-614) says a skipping ignore would not validate escapes or number range. What survives: a macro or shared helper for the repeated default visit_* methods of LenientString, LenientU64, LenientPayload and RawResult, and folding `acknowledgement` into parse_typed. Note that `acknowledgement` is called from relay.rs:1965 and several tests.
evidence: An Ack has four fields: id, verdict, rewound and last_seq. The file is 769 lines, and lines 129-695 are custom Deserialize/Visitor impls for RawAck, RawPayload, LenientPayload, RawResult, LenientString, LenientU64 and Validate. LenientString (431-520) and LenientU64 (522-610) are about 90 lines each and differ only in which visit_* method keeps its value. Validate (616-695, 80 lines) visits every JSON type and discards it, which is what serde::de::IgnoredAny does when passed as the visitor to `deserialize_any`: serde_json still decodes string escapes and checks number range on that path. `acknowledgement` (ack.rs:112) only forwards to `parse_typed`.
prop: Write one generic `Lenient<T>` whose Deserialize tries T and otherwise drains the value with `deserializer.deserialize_any(IgnoredAny)`. title: From<CliError> for Failure lists about 115 variants by hand only to call the same body that From<&CliError> already has
reason: error.rs:951-1074 is a Forwarded arm plus an or-pattern of 110 CliError variants. Its body is the same as From<&CliError> at 1076-1085, and the debt comment at 953 says it is meant to become a passthrough plus Failure::from(&other). docs/code-quality/lints.md (lines 77-80) says a match that handles one variant and ignores the rest uses `if let`, and that `if let` trips none of the wildcard lints. So the proposed form follows the repo's own rule, and code() still matches every variant exhaustively. About 112 lines go.
evidence: The match at error.rs:953-1072 has one Forwarded arm and one or-pattern that names every other CliError variant, about 115 lines of variant names, ending in Failure { code: other.code(), message: other.to_string(), .. }. That body is exactly From<&CliError> for Failure at error.rs:1076-1085. The 'debt:' comment on line 952 admits the match is temporary. Each new error variant must be added in three places: the enum, code() at 635-750, and this list. The list adds no exhaustiveness check that code() does not already give.
prop: Write it as `if let CliError::Forwarded(failure) = error { return failure; } Failure::from(&error)`. An if-let is not a match, so the wildcard lints do not fire, and the exhaustive match in code() still makes every new variant pick a code.

title: prune re-derives the same five-part selection, key sets, byte total and removal sequence in three functions
reason: The repetition is real. Each of prune_run (356-363), select_for_hub (569-576) and remove_for_hub (705-748) selects all five parts. The would-free sum appears twice (384-388 and 611-615). The key sets are built twice. The match that keeps Deletable and Continues rows appears four times (595-603, 652-660, 980-988, 1043-1061). print_rows is called three times with the same seven arguments, after the up-front terminal check, so it can be hoisted. The failure tuple appears in 6 signatures. But the three selections are not identical. worktrees::select_scoped gets dry_run=args.dry_run, true and false, which decides whether the worktree locks are held. remove_for_hub selects diagnostics first and holds the locks on purpose, as its comments say. So a single Plan needs a lock or dry-run parameter and must keep the reselect-before-removal order. The home.join("logs") versus config::logs_dir difference is only spelling. 110 lines is optimistic; about 70 is realistic.
evidence: prune_run (prune.rs:356-363), select_for_hub (569-576) and remove_for_hub (713-748) each call log::started_sessions, sessions::select_scoped, worktrees::select_scoped, pinned::select_scoped and old_diagnostics twice. prune_run reads home.join("logs") while the other two read config::logs_dir(home). The would-free sum of five terms appears twice (384-388 and 611-615). The previewed key sets (removal.dir.display(), removal.hash, file.path.display()) are built twice (select_for_hub 618-632, remove_for_hub 720-736). The order 'diagnostics, then worktrees, then pinned' with freed and failures added up is written twice (prune_run 414-425, remove_for_hub 779-800). The match that picks out a Deletable or Continues row and skips Blocked, Cycle and Unreadable is written four times (595-603, 652-660, 980-988, 1043-1061). print_rows is called three times in prune_run with the same seven arguments (370, 390, 401). Failures travel as an untyped (String, ErrorCode, String) tuple in 6 signatures across prune.rs, pinned.rs and worktrees.rs.
prop: Add a prune Plan type that is selected once for a Scope: plan.lines(now), plan.keys(), plan.would_free(), plan.retain(&want), and plan.remove(home, clock) returning a Removed { freed, failures: Vec<PruneFailure>, total }. Add SessionRow::deletable() -> Option<(&id, &dir, bytes, delete)>. prune_run, select_for_hub and remove_for_hub would then differ only in how they connect and send deletes. print_rows can move above the dry-run branch and be called once.

title: fiber mcp add flattens main's typed McpDeclaration back into strings and validates transport states the enum already rules out
reason: main.rs:543-575 splits -e on its first '=' and enforces exactly one transport, and no env or secret with a url, before it builds McpDeclaration. mcp_add (mcp.rs:696-706) calls split_declaration (430-453) to rebuild KEY=value strings. run_add (281-320) then checks the transport again: McpUrlAndCommand, McpTransportMissing and McpUrlWithEnv. split_env (108-120) splits the strings again and can raise McpEnvPair. grep shows no other product caller of run_add or split_env, and none of those four variants outside mcp.rs and error.rs (only code() and the From list). No doc names them. Keep check_env_key and McpProgramMissing, since the declaration can still hold an empty program string. About 65 lines go, before the test rewrites.
evidence: main::mcp_declaration (main/src/main.rs:544-575) splits each -e on '=' and enforces 'exactly one transport, no -e or --secret with a url' before it builds McpDeclaration::{Remote, Stdio}. cli::mcp_add then calls split_declaration (mcp.rs:430-453), which joins the env pairs back into 'KEY=value' strings and returns a 4-tuple (Option<&str>, Vec<String>, Vec<String>, Vec<String>). run_add (281) checks the transport again: McpUrlAndCommand, McpTransportMissing and McpUrlWithEnv (mcp.rs:305-316). split_env (108-120) splits the strings again and raises McpEnvPair. prop: Have run_add take &McpDeclaration and build declaration_value from it. Delete split_declaration, the transport match and the '=' split in split_env (keep check_env_key), and the McpUrlAndCommand, McpTransportMissing, McpUrlWithEnv and McpEnvPair variants together with their arms in code() and the From list. title: The config-loading step 'project_of, then Config::load(Sources { home, workspace, project, overrides })' is written out 21 times in 13 files
reason: There are 19 Config::load(Sources{..}) sites in cli product code, not 21; lib.rs:228 is project_key_for_identity, not a load. There are 29 project_of calls. evidence: There are 21 Config::load(Sources { .. }) sites. title: Test-only code and test-only visibility live in product files: a 237-line doctor test seam, five cfg(test) prune wrappers, and about 44 crate-visible items named only by tests
reason: What holds: doctor/files.rs is 520 lines, with a no-op seam at 262-282 and a cfg(test) seam at 284-520. The five cfg(test) prune wrappers exist (sessions.rs:93, pinned.rs:100 and 134, worktrees.rs:121 and 458); 33 test call sites use select or select_with. login.rs:711 is a cfg(test) reviewer_stage. Spot checks agree that the named examples are only used inside their own file plus its child test modules (run_local and run_remote in stop.rs:76/87, render_text and render_json in hub_status.rs:61/63, provider_offers, model_offers, shell_from_env and completions_installed in setup.rs), and those test modules are children that can see private items. What is overstated: moving the doctor seam to another file moves 237 lines but removes none. The thread_local hooks in stop.rs:157-205 and hub_service.rs:165-200 fire inside the product flow (for example stop.rs:199), so they cannot leave the file. Making items private removes no lines. I could not re-count the 44 of 153 figure. Only the wrappers, about 60 lines, are actually removed.
evidence: doctor/files.rs:262-520 holds a no-op `mod seam` for production and a 237-line #[cfg(test)] `mod seam` (284-520), with six static Mutex gate lists, Pause and ChunkPause guards and arm_*/take_* functions. That inflates the product file to 520 lines when its real code is about 260. prune has five #[cfg(test)] 'workspace form' wrappers that exist only so old tests keep calling select(..workspace..): sessions::select (94-110), pinned::select (101-108), pinned::select_with (135-152), worktrees::select (122-140) and worktrees::scope_keys (459-461). hub_service.rs:166-200 and stop.rs:158-205 carry thread_local hooks used only by tests, and login.rs:711 has a cfg(test) reviewer_stage. A per-item scan found that 44 of the slice's 153 pub(crate)/pub(super) items (not counting the doctor seam) are named by no other product file, only by their own module's tests. Examples are mcp::run_add, run_remove, run_list and split_declaration; hub_status::render_text and render_json; setup::provider_offers, model_offers, shell_from_env and completions_installed; and stop::run_local and run_remote. A #[path] test module is a child module and can already see private items, so these do not need wider visibility. docs/code-quality.md (Visibility, Size) says an item is private unless another module needs it, and that unit tests live in their own file so a file's length is its code.
prop: Move the cfg(test) seam into doctor/files_tests.rs or a test_support file, leaving only the no-op call sites in product code. Have the prune tests call select_scoped(.., Scope::Project(ws), ..) and delete the five wrappers. Make the 44 test-only pub(crate) items private.

title: The extension entry points repeat the home-and-terminal setup five times instead of using with_dirs
reason: The five entry points (extension.rs:130-272) do open-code fiber_home_from_env().map_err(..).and_then, and four build the same Io literal. But with_dirs_code (lib.rs:303-317) always reads the current directory, while extension_install without --project, extension_update and extension_reinstall never read it today. Routing them through it would make a missing current directory fail those commands. It also reports that failure as Forwarded IoFailed with a different message, where today it is CliError::ExtensionDirectory with its own code (error.rs:395, 881). So only remove and list fit with_dirs as it stands. An Io::stdio constructor plus a home-only helper would save about 20 lines.

title: The session Gate is a wide, reach-into struct with a dozen setter/getter pairs
reason: Gate (session.rs:94-208) does have 17 pub(crate) fields. Ten setters at session.rs:451-589 follow the `set` plus `debug_assert!("... wired once")` pattern, plus close_now at 656. That is 11 such setters, not 12. A twelfth assert, for `cancel` at 320, sits inside `run`, and `history` is filled with `get_or_init` in `serve`, so neither is a public setter. Each slot has a trivial `.get().cloned()` getter (session.rs:970-1043). `envelope(&gate.session_id, gate.clock.as_ref(), ..)` really does appear 10 times: client.rs 743, 1333, 1340, 1417, 1429, 1475; level.rs 142, 161; writer.rs 307; shell.rs 99. Files outside session.rs that touch Gate fields directly: I count 11 (artifact, client, client/level, client/writer, drive, message, notes, offered, prompt_history, session/accept, shell), not 13. Several claims are wrong. Not every setter is called from session_command.rs: close_now is wired from crates/main/src/shutdown.rs:91. `sealed` has no getter; it is pub(crate) only because session_tests.rs:4283 reads it. `personal_source_check` is reached outside session.rs only through its getter (client.rs:516). The doors/tests/socket.rs tests call setters such as close_now one at a time on an already opened session, so a Wiring struct handed to run/serve changes the public API and every one of those tests. The idea is workable, but 130 lines is too high once the struct, its Default and the test rewrites are counted.
evidence: `Gate` has 17 pub(crate) fields (log, clock, session_id, tools, rate, personal_source_check, accepted, steering, pasting, history, prompts, home, dir, admission, shells, sealed, conns). Other files read them directly: `gate.clock` and `gate.session_id` in 5 files each, `gate.home` in 4, `gate.conns` in 4, `gate.log` in 5. In all, 13 product files outside session.rs touch Gate fields. About 12 optional collaborators sit in OnceLock slots (quota, credentials, servers_refresh, mcp_login, personal_source_check, jobs, repository, images, close_now, driver_shell, notes_workspace, history). Each has a public `Session::x(...)` setter whose body is `set` plus `debug_assert!("x is wired once")` (12 copies, session.rs:459-596). Each also has a pub(crate) `Gate::x()` getter that is just `.get().cloned()` (session.rs:959-1043). Two fields are both pub(crate) and behind a getter: `personal_source_check`, and `sealed`, which no other file uses. In production all the setters are called from one place, crates/main/src/session_command.rs:899-1024. In addition, `session::envelope(&gate.session_id, gate.clock.as_ref(), &event)` is spelled out at 10 call sites in client.rs, client/level.rs, client/writer.rs and shell.rs.
prop: Make `Gate` a deeper module. (1) Replace the 12 OnceLock slots and their setter/getter pairs with one plain `Wiring` struct of `Option` fields. The session process fills it once and hands it over before `run`/`serve`; tests build it with `..Default::default()`. (2) Add `Gate::envelope(&Event)` and make `session_id` and `clock` private. (3) Make `personal_source_check` and `sealed` private. Command handlers would then ask the Gate for what they need, not read its fields.

title: SessionError's two Failure conversions and its hand-written Debug are copy-paste
reason: Line numbers are about 10 lower than the real ones. The owned conversion is at session_error.rs:204-236, the borrowed one at 238-270, and Debug at 276-356. Both conversions list the same 19 variants and differ only in `failure` versus `failure.clone()`. Debug writes out all 20 variants to hide the worktree::Error source; the reason is the redaction rule in docs/code-quality.md:104, and the test at session_error_tests.rs:310 checks it. The proposed `other => Failure::from(&other)` arm would not compile: a binding arm counts as a wildcard, and Cargo.toml:73 denies `wildcard_enum_match_arm`. It has to be written as `if let SessionError::Forwarded(f) = error { return f; } Failure::from(&error)`. The newtype-plus-derive plan works if the newtype implements Error and forwards `source()`, and `code()` (line 194) reaches through it. The two construction sites at isolation.rs:80 and 399 and the two at 172 and 189 must wrap the value. The derived Debug would also drop the extra `code` field that WorktreeFailed prints today (line 334); no test checks it.
evidence: `From<SessionError> for Failure` (lines 194-221) and `From<&SessionError> for Failure` (lines 224-252) both list the same 19 variants and build the same Failure. They differ only in `failure` versus `failure.clone()` for `Forwarded`. The `Debug` impl (lines 258-355, about 97 lines) writes out all 20 variants by hand. Its only purpose is to leave out the `worktree::Error` source on `WorktreeFailed` and `WorktreeAccess`.
prop: Make the owned conversion `match error { Forwarded(f) => f, other => Failure::from(&other) }`. Wrap the two worktree sources in a small newtype whose `Debug` hides the content but which still forwards `source()`, then `#[derive(Debug)]` on the enum.

title: The first subscribe and a level change each prepare a subscription their own way
reason: The overlap is real. Both functions do the watch / watch_all_seeded preparation (client.rs:666-694, level.rs:130-174), set conn.full and attach or detach, and settle the credential the same way (client.rs:710-721, level.rs:198-211). The Subscribe acceptance is built three times (client.rs:743, client.rs:1417 inside settle_response, level.rs:161). The Direct sink is put back three times (client.rs:670, 765, 776). But the preparations differ in ways a shared `prepare` would have to carry. A summary level change records `cutoff = log.count()` (level.rs:137); the first subscribe does not. A summary level change accepts with `result: None` (level.rs:142-148), while a first summary subscribe accepts with Subscribe{last_seq}. The first full subscribe has a test probe point (client.rs:689-691). One function writes the acceptance straight to the socket, the other publishes it as a prelude through the writer. The constructor and the sink-restore helper are clean wins. A single `prepare` saves less than 60 lines.
evidence: `subscribe` (client.rs:653-806, about 150 lines) and `level::change` (client/level.rs:115-243, about 130 lines) contain the same steps. For summary they call `log.watch()` plus `latest("session_status")` and `latest("extensions_loaded")` (client.rs:677-681 and level.rs:136-139). For full they call `log.watch_all_seeded()`. Both set `conn.full` and attach or detach. With a credential, both call `settle_response`, `outbox.settle(cancel)` and deliver `Delivery::Credential` (client.rs:715-724 and level.rs:203-209). The acceptance `CommandAccepted { result: last_seq.map(|last_seq| CommandResult::Subscribe { last_seq, workspace_gone: None }) }` is built in three places: client.rs:743, client.rs:1417 and level.rs:161. In `subscribe`, the step that puts the `Direct` sink back on failure is written three times (client.rs:672, 763, 773).
prop: Extract one `prepare(log, level) -> Prepared { watcher, injector, cutoff, snapshots }`, one `subscribe_accepted(id, last_seq)` constructor, and one `submit_switch(conn, label, last_seq) -> Receiver`. `subscribe` and `change` would keep only what actually differs: writing straight to the socket versus switching through the writer.

title: sessions.rs hand-rolls the same non-blocking socket line reader three times
reason: These are confirmed as written: the wake-pair setup is word for word the same at sessions.rs:272-281 and 561-570, apart from the error mapper (io_error versus message_io). The summary-subscribe literal appears at sessions.rs:140, 307, 545 and attach.rs:247. The guarded_connect closure is also duplicated (292-297 and 494-499). The three readers are not one pipeline, though. The probe reads one stream through BufReader and fill_buf, waits with hub::wait_ready, and carries a mutants exemption (178-182). The listing multiplexes many connections in one poll set through an injected `read` seam. The message exchange interleaves partial writes with reads through the ExchangeIo seams. The cap checks also mean different things: total bytes over the cap is InvalidData (196), buffer length minus the cap is above zero (437), and a newline position past the cap (630, 649). A single `LineConn::poll_lines` would have to absorb the injected seams and the multiplexing. The wake_pair, summary_subscribe and connect helpers save about 30-40 lines; a unified line reader is not shown to fit.
evidence: Three functions each do their own connect, send a summary subscribe, then poll and split lines. They are `probe_socket` plus `probe_line` (lines 113-220, about 105 lines), `list_until_with_read` (lines 243-443, about 200 lines) and `message_exchange` (lines 527-654, about 128 lines). The wake socket-pair setup (pair, two `set_nonblocking` calls, `Waker`, `clock.subscribe`, `cancel.subscribe`) is word for word the same at 271-281 and 562-570. The 'drain to newline, cap at MAX_LINE, parse Value' step appears at 189-215, 395-437 and 625-650, with three different cap checks. The `Command::Subscribe(SubscribeArgs { level: Summary, credential: None })` literal is built at sessions.rs:137, 297 and 546, and again in attach.rs:243.
prop: Add one private `LineConn` type that owns a non-blocking stream, its pending buffer and the MAX_LINE cap, with `poll_lines(...) -> impl Iterator<Value>`. Add one `wake_pair(clock, cancel)` helper and one `summary_subscribe(id)` constructor. The probe, the listing and the message exchange then contain only their own stage logic.

title: The in-process driver re-implements the socket line pipeline with hand-built rejections
reason: drive.rs:56-128 repeats on_line (client.rs:231-263): classify, then reserve, then the subscribe check, then parse. After the gate upgrade it builds six rejections by hand (73, 82, 90, 99, 110, 120) and calls `accepted.release` by hand three times (98, 109, 119). `reject` (client.rs:1308-1322) already releases the id, except for malformed and duplicate, which matches what the driver does by hand. It sends through `send`, whose `Sink::Driven` branch (1344) routes the rejection to the host Ack. So building `Conn::driven` (drive.rs:227) first and routing through reject keeps the behaviour. A driven Conn counts as subscribed (`subscribed()` at client.rs:104 is false only for Direct), so a shared admit step passes the not-subscribed check, and the driver keeps its own `subscribe` refusal and approval/offer-reply refusal. The closing rejection before the gate upgrade (drive.rs:60-65) has to stay hand-built. About 30 lines.
evidence: `Driver::drive` (drive.rs:55-126) repeats `on_line`'s steps (client.rs:231-262): classify, then `accepted.reserve`, then the subscribe check, then `parse`, then `dispatch`. Because no `Conn` exists yet at that point, it writes `answer.0(Err(Rejection { code, message: X.to_owned() }))` by hand 6 times, and calls `accepted.release` by hand 3 times. The `reject` used by the socket path already handles releasing the id. `Conn::driven` is only built at the very end (drive.rs:124). Both paths also check the command name as the text "subscribe" (drive.rs:96, client.rs:246).
prop: Build the driven `Conn` first. Move classify, reserve and parse into one `client::admit_line(conn, bytes) -> Option<(CommandLine, String)>` that both paths call. The driver keeps only its two extra refusals (subscribe and person-only replies) and expresses them through `reject`.

title: client.rs is 1524 lines; the session-socket refusal policy is a separate module inside it
reason: client.rs is 1524 lines. The attribution and refusal code really is a separable block (Attribution at 1004 through session_command_refusal ending at 1303), and docs/code-quality.md:162-181 treats a file over 800 lines as one to split, so the move is supported. title: Closed sets travel as text even though enums for them exist
reason: Accepted stores ids as String (accepted.rs:21, 35, 38). `answered` and `resolve` take `&str` and compare `code == Some("malformed")` (accepted.rs:94-95, 112-113). The writer pulls the values out of the payload JSON (writer.rs:359-363). The claim that the writer 'already has' typed values is wrong: it holds a generic Envelope payload Value, not a parsed CommandAccepted or CommandRejected, so it would still read the JSON and then wrap the result in CommandId and ErrorCode. `is_answer` call sites: I count 8, not 9 (sessions.rs 413, 640, 643; steer.rs 178, 181, 190; attach.rs 281, 284). `kind(&line) == "session_status"` is at sessions.rs:426. `log.latest("...")` takes &str (log/src/write.rs:322) and appears 5 times, offered.rs:18 included. The census-ratchet rule in docs/code-quality.md:146 does favour enums here. It is a real typing improvement, but it removes almost no lines.
evidence: `Accepted` stores command ids as `String` (accepted.rs:21, 35, 38), though a `CommandId` newtype exists. Its `answered` and `resolve` take `id: &str, code: Option<&str>` and compare `code == Some("malformed")`, though `ErrorCode` exists. The writer gets these values by pulling `command_id` and `code` back out of the JSON payload (writer.rs:359-363). Event kinds are compared as text through `attach::is_answer(line, "command_accepted"|"command_rejected", ..)` at 9 sites (attach.rs:281, 284; steer.rs:178, 181, 190; sessions.rs:415, 640, 643) and `kind(&line) == "session_status"` (sessions.rs:426), even though `EventKind::from_name` exists. `log.latest("session_status")` and `log.latest("extensions_loaded")` appear 4 times (client.rs:679-680, level.rs:138-139).
prop: Make `Accepted` take `&CommandId` and `Option<&ErrorCode>`, which the writer already has once it parses the acknowledgement. Give `is_answer` an `EventKind` parameter and parse the kind name once with `EventKind::from_name`. If the `log` crate's interface allows it, have `latest` take an `EventKind`.

title: dispatch repeats inbox arms; deliver_message forks on a bool flag
reason: The line numbers are about 15 lower than the real ones. The Prompt and Steer arms are at client.rs:364-379 and are identical except for the true/false argument. deliver_message (867-911) branches on that bool between admission plus prompt history and `admit_steer`, and its only callers are those two arms. Compact, ChangeWorkspace and Rewind pass the id as well. evidence: The `Prompt` and `Steer` arms (client.rs:349-364) are the same 7 lines except for a `true`/`false` argument. `deliver_message(.., prompt: bool, ..)` (867-916) then uses that bool to choose between two unrelated paths: admission plus history for a prompt, and `admit_steer` for a steer. title: Hub connect exposes a test hook every caller fills with a no-op, plus a test-only entry point
reason: `connect_until` (hub.rs:85-104) takes `before_read`. Every caller passes `&mut || {}`: cli/src/stop.rs:114, doors/tests/hub.rs:74 and 1246, main/tests/hub_daemon/hub_remote_terminal.rs:228 and main/tests/hub_daemon/hub.rs:563. The other entry points (connect, connect_within, probe_with) also pass `|| {}` into connect_with. The only real hook is in hub_tests.rs:106, which calls the private `read_hello` directly. `before_read` appears 18 times in hub.rs and is threaded through connect_with, attempt, finish_deferred and finish_connect, several of which carry `too_many_arguments` allowances (401, 447, 670, 713). It can be dropped from that whole chain and kept on read_hello. `hub::connect` (61) is called only from tests in crates/main/tests and crates/doors/tests; no product code calls it.
evidence: The public `connect_until(home, start, clock, deadline, before_read)` takes a `before_read` closure. Its only product caller (cli/src/stop.rs:114) and every test caller (doors/tests/hub.rs:74, 1246; main/tests/hub_daemon/hub.rs:563; hub_remote_terminal.rs:228) pass `&mut || {}`. prop: Remove `before_read` from the public `connect_until` and keep the hook only on the private path the unit test drives. Consider making `connect` a test-support helper, or dropping it in favour of `connect_within(.., CONNECT_DEADLINE)`.

title: Fiber-home layout paths are joined by hand next to the config helpers that own them

title: Two copies of the start-a-thread-then-hand-over-the-ack pattern; a third panics instead
reason: shell (client.rs:618-648) and notes::run (notes.rs:37-75) do share the shape: spawn first, reject io_failed with shell::COULD_NOT_START if the spawn fails, then inbox_ack and send. The McpLogin arm (client.rs:472) uses a bare `thread::spawn`, which panics if the thread cannot start; with panic=abort that ends the process. That is a real inconsistency. But the two copies are not identical. shell must call `running.abandon(&conn.gate)` both when the spawn fails and when the send fails, and notes has nothing to clean up. A helper taking `work: impl FnOnce(Ack)` would move `running` into the closure and lose it when the spawn fails, so the proposal as written drops the abandon cleanup. The helper would need an on-failure callback, or a payload it hands back on error. The saving is smaller than 25 lines; fixing McpLogin is the more valuable part.
evidence: `shell` (client.rs:618-651) and `notes::run` (notes.rs:37-76) each make an mpsc channel, spawn a named thread that `recv`s `(work, Ack)`, reject `io_failed` with `shell::COULD_NOT_START` if the spawn fails, then call `inbox_ack` and send, dropping the ack if the send fails. That is about 20 near-identical lines in each. The `McpLogin` arm (client.rs:472) uses a bare `thread::spawn` instead, which panics if the thread cannot start rather than rejecting with `io_failed`.
prop: Add one `client::on_thread(conn, id, name, work: impl FnOnce(Ack))` that does the spawn, the `io_failed` rejection and the hand-over. Use it for shell, notes and mcp_login.

title: The locked read-modify-write of a configuration file is written out about twelve times, and the copies differ in whether they check the file's shape
reason: The duplication is real. I opened write.rs:73, 259, 310, 599, 634, 693, 744, 771 and 847, entries.rs:32 and import.rs:1550. Each one takes the lock, reads the file or falls back, edits it, and calls write_root or serialises by hand. grep finds 15 `locked(` calls in total, because lines.rs:18/48 and notes.rs:223/236 are also callers. The empty-object fallback is written 7 times on write paths, plus once in lib.rs:296, which is a read. The inconsistency is also real: only replace_global (608), clear_global_if_equals (642) and reset (699) run check_layer, and path::set (path.rs:55-61) does replace a non-object root with an empty map. Three parts of the proposal do not work as stated. (1) 'Run the same post-lock shape check every time' is wrong for set_settings_file. It writes an extension settings file, not config.json, so check_layer (lib.rs:842, which applies the config.json key rules) does not apply there; only the top-level-object check does. The check has to depend on which kind of file is being written. (2) notes.rs:639 pretty_bytes does not write a file. It produces the bytes for a convergence comparison, so it cannot call write_root. At most it could share a serialiser with it. (3) The copies return different things when the file is absent or nothing changed (Reset::Absent, Ok(None), previous value, bool), and update_global_entries and write_servers check the shape at the key, not the root. A closure helper still works, but each copy saves about 3 to 5 lines, not 7. Realistic saving is 30 to 40 lines.
evidence: Every write function repeats the same steps: `let _lock = locked(&file)?`, then `read(&file)?.unwrap_or_else(|| Value::Object(Map::new()))` or a `let Some(root) = read(..) else`, then a change through path::set or path::remove, then write_root. The copies are set (write.rs:73-81), set_settings_file (259-267), edit_list (310-321), replace_global (599-622), clear_global_if_equals (634-645), reset (693-708), insert_entry (744-751), remove_entry (771-788), update (847-854), update_global_entries (entries.rs:32-66) and import's write_servers (import.rs:1550-1592). `grep 'locked('` finds 12 product call sites in the crate, and the empty-object fallback is written 8 times. How the file is checked after the lock is taken differs between copies. replace_global (606-609), clear_global_if_equals (642) and reset (699) run check_layer on the root they read, because, as the comment at write.rs:601-605 says, a concurrent write may have left something like `[]`, which path::set 'would silently destroy'. set_settings_file only checks that the top level is an object (260-264). set, edit_list, insert_entry, update, update_global_entries and import's write_servers do not check at all, even though path::set (path.rs:55-61) replaces a non-object root with a new object. write_root's serialisation (pretty-print, add a newline, atomic write) is written out again in import.rs:1586-1591 and in notes.rs:639-645 (pretty_bytes).
prop: Add one private function in write.rs, for example `edit_file(file, source, |root| -> Result<bool>)`. It would take the lock, read the file or start from an empty object, run the same post-lock shape check every time, call the closure, and write only when the closure reports a change. Every function listed above becomes a closure passed to it. That removes the repeated steps and makes all of them guard the file the same way. import's write_servers and notes' pretty_bytes should call write_root, or the new function, instead of serialising by hand.

title: Which files make up a layer, and whether a repository layer exists, is worked out separately in a dozen functions, and callers must run the existence check themselves first
reason: Confirmed. Ten functions in write.rs take home/workspace/project (lines 50, 112, 211, 233, 302, 480, 509, 670, 719, 761), plus switches.rs:137 and editable.rs:11. refuse_overlapping_repository runs at write.rs:55 and again at 121 on the same set() path, and in insert_entry and remove_entry (725, 766). edit_list and reset never call it, which is a real gap. The plain() checks are written twice (140-142 and 521-522). same_repository_home (lib.rs:712) canonicalises on every call. Hand-written `home.join("projects").join(project...)` appears 7 times outside layout.rs plus about 5 inside it. Overstated: the CLI's three calls are not redundant. cli/src/config.rs:193 runs before project_of() and check_model. cli/src/mcp.rs:301 runs before argument validation and before secrets are read from the terminal. They make the command fail before the person is prompted or any work is done. Moving the refusal into layer_file would remove those calls only if the CLI builds the layer value up front and asks it first. So the refusal still has to be reachable from the CLI before the write. The rest of the proposal is sound, but 70 lines is high; about 40 is realistic.
evidence: 12 product functions in the crate take the same three parameters, `home: &Path, workspace: &Path, project: &ProjectKey`: set, set_extension_setting, settings_layer_file, set_repo_extension_setting, edit_list, Layer::source, layer_file and reset in write.rs, insert_entry and remove_entry in write.rs, switch_skill (switches.rs:134), and is_editable_config_path (editable.rs:8). Sources (lib.rs:115) and ExtensionSettings (extension_settings.rs:22-25) already hold the same three values. refuse_overlapping_repository is public. cli/src/config.rs:193 calls it and then calls config::set, which calls it again at write.rs:55 and a third time in set_extension_setting at write.rs:121. cli/src/mcp.rs:301 and :489 call it before insert_entry and remove_entry, which call it again at write.rs:725 and :766. edit_list (299) and reset (667) never call it. same_repository_home, which canonicalises two paths on every call, is called at lib.rs:264, 674 and 729, extension_settings.rs:123 and 273, and write.rs:495. The plain-file checks on the repository layer are written twice: write.rs:140-142 and 521-522. layout.rs has projects_dir but no function for one project's directory, so `home.join("projects").join(project.as_str())` is written by hand 12 times: 7 inside layout.rs, plus prompt_files.rs:26, extension_settings.rs:114, 193 and 270, write.rs:217, lib.rs:240 and rules.rs:117. `workspace.join(".fiber")` is written 15 times in the crate.
prop: Add one value that knows where the layers are, built once from home, workspace and project. Sources minus its overrides would do. It would answer each Layer's config file and settings directory, whether a repository layer exists (canonicalising once), and the plain-file checks. Its layer_file method would make the overlapping-repository refusal itself, so refuse_overlapping_repository stops being public and the CLI's three calls go away. The write functions, switch_skill and ExtensionSettings would take this value instead of three loose parameters. Add `layout::project_dir(home, project)` for the hand-written paths.

title: Routing gives main five small pieces for reading a provider's access, and main assembles them in four places
reason: The connect half holds. connect and connect_observed (connect.rs:115-147) are thin wrappers over build. Three callers branch on Option<diag> to pick one or the other: reviewer.rs:111-130 and switch.rs:774-792 do; switch.rs:501 calls connect only. Taking `Option<&Diagnostics>` removes about 15 to 20 lines. The access half is overstated. The four assemblies are not the same nesting. parts.rs:604-643 first runs a has_credential check and falls back to session_credential for its diagnostic. parts.rs:676 reads a per-provider cache map first and fills it. switch.rs:587-633 may start the Lua package, uses a `known` key, exempts the current label from the asked-label check (`want.label != current`), and keeps `read.file`. switch/quota.rs:473 loops over labels and has no scripted check. The two asked-label checks differ, since switch.rs exempts the current label and parts.rs:629 does not. One `routing::access` function would need parameters for cache, known key, Lua start and file capture, so main's four sites would not shrink to one call each. scripted.rs does export the five small functions, plus prepare.
evidence: scripted.rs exports five functions of 2 to 10 lines each (is_scripted, access, label, credential, warm). Each one asks 'is this the scripted provider?' for a different step, and main has to call each at the right moment: parts.rs:564, 604, 676, 804 and 924; switch.rs:587, 720 and 886; delegates.rs:555; switch/labels.rs:40; reload.rs:557. Reading access always nests the same calls: scripted::access, then lua_providers::session_credential, then credential::session_credential or credential::switch_credential, then Access::new. main writes this nesting at parts.rs:604-643, parts.rs:676-688, switch.rs:587-633 and switch/quota.rs:473-478. The check that an asked-for label exists, ending in no_label, is written by hand in both parts.rs:629-637 and switch.rs:614-621. credential::session_credential and switch_credential (credential.rs:69-104) differ only in how they pick the label and whether they keep `file`. Every connect caller takes Access apart into key, signer and `lua.map(|l| (l, label))`, then branches on Option<diag> to choose connect or connect_observed: reviewer.rs:111-130, switch.rs:774-792 and switch.rs:501-507. Inside routing, connect and connect_observed (connect.rs:115-144) are both thin wrappers over build, which already takes Option<&Diagnostics>.
prop: Give routing one function for reading access, for example `routing::access(config, provider, lua, label, key_source) -> Result<(String, Access), Failure>`. It would own the scripted short-circuit, the asked-label check, the Lua credential token and the stored-key read. Change connect to take `&Access`, the label and `Option<&Diagnostics>`, and drop connect_observed. Most of scripted.rs then becomes private to routing, and main's four assemblies shrink to one call each.

title: connect.rs builds five protocol branches that are copies of each other except for the type
reason: I opened connect.rs:243-323. There are five branches: Responses, Completions, Messages, Gemini and Converse. Each builds the protocol (with a cache_key_header match in four of them and deferred_tools in Responses and Messages) and then makes the same `diag.and_then(|diag| observed(diag, &here.clock, x.clone(), X::call_observed, here.cache_diagnostics))` call before `(Arc::new(x), observe)`. observed (156-165) is already generic over P. A generic helper that takes the protocol value and its call_observed would turn each branch into a construction plus one call. cache_key_header can stay as a per-branch match, or go behind a small trait. Saving is about 40 lines, not 50, because each protocol still needs its own construction.
evidence: Lines 243-323 hold five match branches of 13 to 17 lines each, 81 lines in all. Each one builds the protocol with `match cache_key_header { Some(name) => X::new(endpoint).cache_key_header(name), None => X::new(endpoint) }`, optionally adds `.deferred_tools(..)`, and then makes the same `diag.and_then(|diag| observed(diag, &here.clock, x.clone(), X::call_observed, here.cache_diagnostics))` call. The branches differ only in the type name and in whether deferred_tools is applied (Responses and Messages).
prop: Write one generic helper, for example `fn erased<P: Provider + Clone + Send + Sync + 'static>(p: P, call: fn(&P, ..), diag, here) -> (Arc<dyn Provider>, Option<Observe>)`, and apply cache_key_header through a small trait that the four protocols that support it already fit, or through a closure passed per branch. Each branch then shrinks to two or three lines.

title: ExtensionSettings walks the same three layer files twice, and their paths are built in four places
reason: I opened extension_settings.rs:100-178 and 255-310. merged and get_layered each build the three settings paths by hand (106-119 and 267-272), each skip the repository when same_repository_home is true (123 and 273), each use the overlay instead of the repository file (126-148 and 275-279), and each filter to repo_settings (156-171, and repository_subtree at 336-348). title: Reading a credential repeats the source lookup that locate() has already done, and the stored credential name is worked out 11 times
reason: The stored-name part is confirmed. `credential_name.as_deref().unwrap_or(...)` appears 11 times in product code (credential.rs:179 and 272-274; credential_origin.rs:117, 258 and 317; extensions/src/lua_provider.rs:57, as a clone variant; cli login.rs:249; doctor/startup.rs:421; logout.rs:35, 46 and 139), so a `stored_name()` helper would work. The claim that lines 210-222 can simply go is wrong. When locate() returns Located::Stored but read_credential then returns None, because the file vanished between the check and the read, credential_through falls through to the source lookup at 210-216. That path has no source in hand, so the lookup is not redundant there. It can be shared, by having Located::Source carry its source and calling configured_source for the fallback, and the duplicated message (195-198 and 218-221) can become one closure. The lines cannot be deleted outright.
evidence: credential_through calls self.locate(), which returns Located::Source(source) (credential_origin.rs:264-273). It then throws the source away (`Located::Source(_) => false`, credential.rs:193) and works it out again at lines 210-216 with the same sources_in().find() and the same `label == DEFAULT_LABEL` fallback to the provider's own source. The error message 'nothing is stored in credentials/{stored}/{label}, and no source is configured for it. The labels for `{name}` are: {listed}' is built twice, at credential.rs:195-198 and 218-221. configured_source (credential.rs:113-122) is the same sources_in().find() as lines 210-213. `provider.credential_name.as_deref().unwrap_or(&provider.name)` is written 11 times: credential.rs:179 and 272, credential_origin.rs:117, 258 and 317, extensions/src/lua_provider.rs:57, cli/src/login.rs:249 (already a private stored_name helper), cli/src/doctor/startup.rs:421, and main/src/configure/logout.rs:35, 46 and 139.
prop: Match on what locate() returns: `Located::Source(source)` already carries the source, so lines 210-222 can go, along with the second copy of the message. Add `ProviderData::stored_name(&self) -> &str` in extension.rs and replace all 11 derivations with it, including cli's private helper.

title: The reasons a key's write scope refuses a layer are written twice, and the 'check the value, refuse on any notice' code is copied five times
reason: The mapping is duplicated. keys.rs:1290-1308 and write.rs:533-548 encode the same WriteScope-by-Source reasons. The wording differs slightly: walk gives the stem ('a repository may not set') and refused_why adds 'it'. refused_why also covers an unknown key ('this Fiber does not know it'), so a shared `refusal()` should return the stem and refused_why should add its own suffix and the unknown case. The checked-then-refuse sequence is at write.rs:65-72, 685-692 and 455-463, and insert_entry (731-743) inlines checked. The apply_edit branches repeat check_list followed by path::set. The proposal does not fit import as stated. import.rs:1530-1548 checks several servers in one candidate and uses its own reason ('this Fiber does not know one entry'), so a single-key checked_or_refused would not cover it without change. Saving is about 30 lines.
evidence: keys.rs walk (1290-1308) maps WriteScope and Source to a sentence: 'a repository may not set', 'only a repository's own file may set', 'only Fiber home's config.json may set', and 'only ... or the project's config.json in Fiber home may set'. write.rs refused_why (533-548) writes the same mapping again with the same sentences, because, as its comment says, 'keys names no reason of its own'. title: Tool trait has three telescoping run entry points, but the loop calls only the third
reason: I opened contract/src/tool.rs:138-169. `run` is required, `run_asking` defaults to `run`, and `run_with_effects` defaults to `run_asking`. The only production callers are loop/src/calls.rs:509 and inner_calls.rs:501, and both call run_with_effects. I count 28 product `impl Tool` blocks. Without the wrappers Capped (loop/caps.rs), LiveSpawn and LiveModels (main/delegates.rs) that leaves 25, as the finding says. Ten of them override a later method, not nine, because extension_tools.rs has two overrides (LuaTool:151 and ProcessTool:234). reviewer_notes_save.rs:109 returns ProgrammeDriven, and fork.rs:77 forwards with None, as claimed. One detail is overstated: ask_user and reviewer_notes_save do reach their own `run`, as a fallback when `!ask.answerable()`. The finding also misses a hazard that supports it. main/delegates.rs:299 and :355 (LiveSpawn, LiveModels) forward only `run` to `fresh()`. That is correct today only because DelegateSpawn and DelegateModels override nothing, which shows how easy it is to wrap the wrong layer. A single `run(Call)` would work. The cost is that the many tests calling `tool.run(&args, ...)` directly would need a Call builder. That moves lines around in tests rather than removing them, so the net saving is mostly the product code, about 70 lines.
evidence: Tool has a required `run(arguments, cancel, emit)`. It also has `run_asking` (adds `ask`, default forwards to run) and `run_with_effects` (adds `effects`, default forwards to run_asking). The only production callers are crates/loop/src/calls.rs:509 and inner_calls.rs:501, and both call run_with_effects; loop/src/caps.rs:76,88 is a wrapper that forwards. Of the 25 product Tool implementations, 9 override run_asking or run_with_effects (extensions extension_tools, jobs delegate/fork, jobs delegate/message, jobs tool, tools reviewer_notes_save, tools ask_user, tools shell, mcp resources, mcp tool). Each of these still has to write a `run` that the loop never reaches. reviewer_notes_save.rs:109 just returns an error, and fork.rs:77, mcp tool.rs:137 and resources.rs:216 forward to an inner helper with `None` for the ask. An implementer has to know which layer the loop really calls.
prop: Collapse the three methods into one `fn run(&self, call: Call<'_>) -> Output`. `Call` would bundle arguments, effects, cancel, emit and ask. Tools that ignore ask or effects simply do not read those fields. Tests that call `tool.run(&args, ...)` directly would build a `Call` with a no-op ask (fakes-contract can provide one). This removes two trait methods and their docs (~30 lines in contract), the 9 forwarding or unreachable `run` bodies, and the caps.rs forwarding pair.

title: Every provider send has a plain path and an observed twin that copy each other
reason: The anchors hold. post_signed (http.rs:139-155) and post_signed_observed (474-527) are twins, and so are status_error (362-391) and observed_status_error (529-588). The observed error read rebuilds ureq's lossy decoding (is_text_body, decode_error_body, lossy_question at 590-650) and its timeout check (read_timed_out, 652-665), and the comments say this is so the body matches the plain path 'byte for byte'. In call.rs, open (391) sits beside open_observed (414-462), and send_plain (502) beside run_observed (569-668). The record is built with ObservationFinish::new, set_redact and set_hashes four times, at 429, 445, 594 and 635. The observed branch of Call::open is reached only from tests (diagnostics.rs:364, http_tests.rs:2357); examples/record/main.rs:101-109 calls plain .open(). One correction: the observed send is used in production through each protocol's call_observed (routing/connect.rs:254-318) at debug level, so there are two live paths, not one live path plus dead code. The deletion list is backwards. The observed path counts bytes underneath ureq's lossy layer, and the comment at 556-561 explains why: ureq reads 8 bytes ahead, which would swallow a short body before a stall. So a single send that always counts has to keep the counted read, meaning decode_error_body, lossy_question and read_timed_out stay. What goes is status_error and ureq's read_to_string. The other choice is to count above the lossy layer and accept a less accurate response_bytes (docs/state.md:302-356 promises 'response_bytes as read'). Folding the four record builders into one helper, and cutting Call::open down to the plain stream, both work as proposed.
evidence: Sending is written twice. In http.rs, post_signed (lines 139-155) has a twin, post_signed_observed (474-527), and status_error (362-391) has a twin, observed_status_error (529-588). The observed path reads the error body through its own counted reader. To keep the two paths in step it re-implements ureq's lossy UTF-8 decoding (is_text_body, decode_error_body and lossy_question, 590-650) and its timeout detection (read_timed_out, 652-665); the comments say this is so 'the body matches the ordinary path's byte for byte'. call.rs repeats the split one level up: open (391) beside open_observed (414-462), and send_plain (503) beside run_observed (569-668). The code that builds the observation record (ObservationFinish::new, then set_redact, then set_hashes when hashes exist) is written out four times, at call.rs:429, 445, 594 and 635. The observed branch of Call::open, which is open_observed plus the finish guard inside OpenBody (676-736), is reached only from tests: crates/provider/tests/diagnostics.rs:364 and http_tests.rs:2357. The one product caller, examples/record/main.rs:101-109, never calls .observed().
prop: Keep one send function in http.rs that always counts bytes and stamps times only when it is given a clock. A counter costs nothing measurable, and with one send there is a single error-body read, so status_error, lossy_question and read_timed_out go. In call.rs, run one path with an Option<ObservationFinish>, built by one helper. Reduce Call::open to the plain stream, or drop it and let the record example use run, which removes OpenBody's guard logic.

title: Tool choice is a String that each protocol reads with a different vocabulary
reason: ModelRequest.tool_choice is a String (contract/src/provider.rs:114), and the same String is stored in the context event (contract/src/events/context.rs:282). The vocabularies are as described: anthropic_messages.rs:444 accepts auto, none and any; openai_completions.rs:235 accepts auto, none and required; google_generative_ai_request.rs:197-200 accepts auto, none and any; bedrock_converse_request.rs:175-176 accepts auto, none and any (none is simply left off the wire); openai_responses.rs:191 inserts the raw string. Every protocol treats any other string as a tool name. docs/code-quality.md:146 says a closed set that crosses a crate boundary must be an enum, so this breaks the rule. One thing to add: every production producer today sets "auto" (loop/reviewer.rs:686, notes.rs:80, and the value carried from the event), so the 'required' and 'any' mix-ups cannot happen yet; they are a latent risk. The fix adds code rather than removing it, and because the value comes from an event, it needs the unknown-name case that docs/code-quality.md:146 describes for event readers.
evidence: ModelRequest.tool_choice is a String that crosses the contract-to-provider crate boundary. Each of the five protocols parses it its own way. Anthropic accepts auto, none and any. Completions accepts auto, none and required. Gemini and Bedrock accept auto, none and any. Responses inserts the raw string unchecked. Every protocol treats any other string as a tool name. As a result, 'required' sent to Anthropic, Gemini or Bedrock forces a tool literally named 'required', and 'any' sent to Completions forces a tool named 'any'. docs/code-quality.md, under 'Types', says a closed set that crosses a crate boundary must be an enum.
prop: In contract, define enum ToolChoice { Auto, None, Required, Tool(String) } and parse it where the value enters. Each protocol then maps the enum to its own wire word with an exhaustive match, and the meaning of 'must call some tool' cannot drift between protocols.
